name: Multiband Communication

name: Indicator Removal from Tools

name: Cached Domain Credentials

name: DCSync
cheat: Look for DRSUAPI/DRSR replication traffic (RPC 135, 49152+) from non-DC hosts or Mimikatz 'lsadump::dcsync' execution. | Distinct from local LSASS dumping: targets remote DC replication APIs to steal hashes (e.g., KRBTGT) without touching local memory.

name: Proc Filesystem
cheat: Monitor root-level reads of /proc/<PID>/mem and /proc/<PID>/maps, often paired with grep/regex for credential patterns. | Distinct from /etc/shadow: extracts live credentials from process virtual memory rather than static hash files.

name: /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow
cheat: Detect cat/unshadow commands targeting /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow, or file creation in /tmp for cracking databases. | Distinct from proc dumping: reads static hash files requiring root, not live process memory.

name: Data from Local System
cheat: Identify bulk file reads, directory traversal, or database queries on local storage (e.g., find, dir, show run) prior to exfiltration. | Distinct from network collection: focuses on local filesystems, configs, and VM files rather than remote sources.

name: Direct Volume Access
cheat: Watch for NinjaCopy, vssadmin, or esentutl usage to create shadow copies or bypass ACLs/monitoring. | Distinct from standard file access: uses direct volume APIs to read/write data, evading file system filters and access controls.

name: SMB/Windows Admin Shares
cheat: SMB traffic to admin shares (C$, ADMIN$, IPC$) or RPC over SMB (port 445) | Distinguishes from T1021.006 by using SMB/RPC protocol rather than WinRM/HTTP

name: Distributed Component Object Model
cheat: DCOM activation via RPC (port 135) or specific COM object CLSIDs (e.g., MMC20, Office) | Distinguishes from T1021.002 by leveraging COM object instantiation rather than direct file share access

name: SSH

name: VNC
cheat: VNC/RFB protocol traffic (port 5900+) or VNC client processes (vncviewer, RealVNC) | Distinguishes from T1021.001 by being screen-sharing (RFB) rather than resource-sharing (RDP)

name: Windows Remote Management
cheat: WinRM service activity (ports 5985/5986) or 'winrm' command execution | Distinguishes from T1021.002 by using HTTP/HTTPS protocol rather than SMB/RPC

name: Command Obfuscation
cheat: Look for command lines with excessive escape characters (^, +, $, %), string concatenation ("Wor"+"d"), or base64 blobs in PowerShell/Bash logs. | Distinguish from T1027.013: obfuscation is in the command string itself, not the file content on disk.

name: Fileless Storage
cheat: Check for payloads stored in Registry, WMI repository, or RAM-backed dirs (/dev/shm, /tmp) instead of persistent disk files. | Distinguish from T1055: data is stored persistently in non-file formats, not injected into another process's memory.

name: LNK Icon Smuggling
cheat: Inspect .LNK files for external URLs in the IconEnvironmentDataBlock field that trigger downloads upon execution. | Distinguish from T1204.002: the malicious payload is hidden in LNK metadata, not the target path itself.

name: Encrypted/Encoded File
cheat: Identify files with high entropy, Base64 content, or SFX/encrypted archives that decode only at runtime. | Distinguish from T1027.002: focus is on encryption/encoding of file bytes, not just packing/compression.

name: Polymorphic Code
cheat: Detect malware samples that change their hash or binary structure between executions while maintaining functionality. | Distinguish from T1027.013: code mutates dynamically at runtime, rather than being statically encrypted/encoded.

name: Compression
cheat: Look for ZIP/gzip/7z/RAR archives in email attachments or C2 downloads; check for concatenated ZIPs (multiple central directories) that evade standard parsers. | Distinguish from encryption: compression reduces size and may be password-protected, but the primary indicator is the archive format and potential self-extracting behavior.

name: Junk Code Insertion
cheat: Identify binaries with high volumes of NOP (0x90) instructions or dead code blocks that do not alter execution flow. | Distinct from Binary Padding: junk code is inserted to hinder static analysis and disassembly, not just to change file hashes or signatures.

name: SVG Smuggling
cheat: Inspect .svg files for embedded <script> tags, JavaScript payloads, or external download URLs disguised as vector graphics. | Distinguish from HTML Smuggling: SVGs are treated as image files by filters/users, allowing malicious JS to bypass content inspection that blocks executable HTML.

name: Invisible Unicode
cheat: Scan text/scripts for zero-width spaces, variation selectors, bidirectional controls, or Private Use Area (PUA) characters that render as blank. | Look for dynamic execution (eval, Proxy) reconstructing payloads from these invisible Unicode code points to evade visual inspection.

name: Scheduled Transfer
cheat: Monitor for exfiltration traffic occurring at consistent, non-business hours or fixed intervals rather than continuous bursts. | Distinguish from other exfil: the key indicator is the temporal scheduling pattern used to blend with normal network activity or availability windows.

name: Data Transfer Size Limits
cheat: Network traffic shows consistent, fixed-size packet chunks or data streams capped below standard alert thresholds. | Distinguish from bulk exfil by the artificial fragmentation pattern designed to evade bandwidth monitoring.

name: System Owner/User Discovery
cheat: Look for execution of whoami, w, who, dscl . list /Users, or environment variable reads like %USERNAME% and $USER. | On network devices, check for CLI commands show users or show ssh to identify active sessions.

name: Path Interception
cheat: Identify executables placed in unquoted service paths (e.g., C:\program.exe instead of C:\program files\app.exe) or directories preceding system32 in PATH. | Deprecated technique; now split into T1574.007 (PATH), T1574.008 (Search Order), and T1574.009 (Unquoted Path).

name: Masquerading
cheat: Malicious files named to mimic legitimate system binaries (e.g., svchost.exe in non-system dirs) or services with benign names. | Includes renaming abusable utilities to evade detection; focus on name/location mismatches with expected behavior.

name: Invalid Code Signature
cheat: Files containing copied signature metadata from legitimate binaries that fail digital signature validation checks. | Distinct from valid code signing (T1553.002) because the signature is invalid but may still deceive users or improperly handled tools.

name: Right-to-Left Override
cheat: Look for U+202E (RTLO) in filenames or registry values; check raw bytes as GUIs may render reversed text (e.g., 'rcs.docx' is actually 'xcod.scr'). | Distinguish from simple typos by verifying if the string reverses when copied to a plain text editor or hex editor.

name: Rename Legitimate Utilities
cheat: Detect legitimate binaries (rundll32, psexec, python) renamed to non-standard names or executed from non-standard paths. | Key distinction: The binary hash matches a known system tool, but the filename or path is anomalous for that specific utility.

name: Masquerade Task or Service
cheat: Inspect Task Scheduler or systemd service names/descriptions for typosquats or exact matches of benign system tasks. | Look for services/tasks with legitimate-looking names but suspicious binary paths or recent creation timestamps.

name: Match Legitimate Resource Name or Location
cheat: Identify executables or registry keys placed in trusted locations (System32, /usr/bin) or named exactly like legitimate resources (svchost.exe). | Distinguish from T1036.003 by the fact that the filename is not renamed but matches a standard system file name, often with a different hash or path context.

name: Space after Filename
cheat: Check for trailing spaces in filenames on macOS/Linux (e.g., 'evil.txt '); the OS ignores the extension and executes the binary based on content. | Look for files with benign extensions that have a single space character at the end of the filename string.

name: Double File Extension
cheat: File names with two extensions where the first is benign (e.g., .txt, .jpg) and the second is executable (e.g., .exe, .lnk, .hta, .scr). | Check file metadata or use 'dir /x' to reveal the true extension hidden by Windows Explorer.

name: Masquerade File Type

name: Break Process Trees
cheat: Processes with PPID 1 (init/systemd) or no parent, often resulting from double-fork() or daemon() syscalls. | Look for orphaned processes detached from their expected parent chain in process trees.

name: Masquerade Account Name
cheat: Newly created accounts with names mimicking legitimate service accounts (e.g., 'backup', 'svc_') or generic terms ('admin', 'root'). | Correlate account creation events with recent account deletions or discovery activities.

name: Overwrite Process Arguments

name: Browser Fingerprint
cheat: HTTP User-Agent header mismatches actual client OS/browser or contains spoofed system attributes (resolution, timezone, language) | Distinguish from standard UA spoofing by presence of full system fingerprint data (e.g., screen size, timezone) crafted to evade browser fingerprinting defenses

name: Boot or Logon Initialization Scripts

name: Systemd Timers
cheat: Identify new .timer and paired .service files in /etc/systemd/system/, /usr/lib/systemd/system/, or ~/.config/systemd/user/; monitor systemctl enable/start commands. | Distinguish from T1053.003 (Cron) by systemd unit file structure and systemctl management instead of crontab entries.

name: Process Injection
cheat: Monitor for cross-process memory writes (WriteProcessMemory), remote thread creation (CreateRemoteThread), or unusual IPC channels like named pipes between unrelated processes. | Distinguish from T1055.001 (DLL Injection) by broader scope including shellcode or raw memory manipulation without necessarily loading a DLL file.

name: Ptrace System Calls

name: Proc Memory
cheat: Monitor for dd or direct writes to /proc/[pid]/maps and /proc/[pid]/mem to overwrite stack or ROP gadgets. | Distinguishes from ptrace by using filesystem interfaces to bypass ASLR and memory protections.

name: Credential API Hooking
cheat: Look for IAT/inline hooking artifacts in process memory or LD_PRELOAD/DYLD_INSERT_LIBRARIES env vars pointing to malicious .so/.dylib | Distinguishes from keylogging by targeting credential-specific API calls (e.g., WTSQueryUserInformation, getpass) rather than raw keystrokes

name: Process Discovery

name: Command and Scripting Interpreter

name: Netsh Helper DLL

name: Accessibility Features

name: AppCert DLLs

name: AppInit DLLs

name: Image File Execution Options Injection

name: PowerShell Profile

name: Emond

name: Component Object Model Hijacking
cheat: Registry CLSID/InprocServer32 or TypeLib keys modified to point to malicious DLLs or 'script:' monikers for remote payloads | Distinguished from DLL Search Order Hijacking by targeting COM object references in HKCR rather than binary load paths

name: Installer Packages

name: Udev Rules

name: Python Startup Hooks

name: Boot or Logon Autostart Execution

name: Registry Run Keys / Startup Folder
cheat: Check HKCU/HKLM\...\CurrentVersion\Run, RunOnce, RunServices, and Policies\Explorer\Run for new values | Inspect C:\Users\*\AppData\Roaming\Microsoft\Windows\Start Menu\Programs\Startup and C:\ProgramData\...\StartUp for dropped executables

name: Authentication Package

name: Time Providers

name: Winlogon Helper DLL
cheat: Audit HKLM/HKCU\...\Winlogon for tampered Userinit, Shell, or Notify subkeys pointing to non-standard paths | Check for unexpected DLL loads by winlogon.exe or userinit.exe during logon

name: Security Support Provider
cheat: Monitor HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Security Packages and OSConfig\Security Packages for added DLL entries | Look for unexpected DLLs loaded into lsass.exe at boot, which grants access to plaintext credentials

name: Kernel Modules and Extensions
cheat: Linux: Check /lib/modules, /sys/module, and dmesg for unexpected LKM loads; macOS: Inspect /Library/Extensions for .kext files and verify signatures via kextstat. Distinguish from T1014 (Rootkit) by focusing on the boot-time loading mechanism rather than active kernel memory hiding.

name: Re-opened Applications
cheat: Inspect ~/Library/Preferences/ByHost/com.apple.loginwindow.[UUID].plist for unexpected application paths added to the 'Reopen windows' list. Distinct from LaunchAgents/Daemons as it relies on the GUI logout/login 'reopen' checkbox behavior rather than direct service registration.

name: LSASS Driver
cheat: Monitor for unauthorized DLLs loaded into lsass.exe or modifications to LSA driver paths in the registry. Distinct from general DLL hijacking (T1574) by specifically targeting the Local Security Authority subsystem for authentication persistence.

name: Shortcut Modification
cheat: Audit .lnk files in Startup folders and user profiles for target path modifications or new shortcuts pointing to malicious binaries. Distinguish from T1036 (Masquerading) by focusing on the shortcut file structure and target redirection rather than file naming alone.

name: Port Monitors
cheat: Check HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Print\Monitors for new subkeys with 'Driver' values pointing to arbitrary DLLs loaded by spoolsv.exe. Distinct from standard service persistence as it leverages the print spooler's monitor loading mechanism at boot.

name: Print Processors
cheat: spoolsv.exe loading DLLs from %WINDIR%\System32\spool\drivers\x64\3\ or registry HKLM\SYSTEM\...\Print\Environments\...\Print Processors\...\Driver | Distinct from standard Run keys: executes at boot via spooler service with SYSTEM privileges, not user logon

name: XDG Autostart Entries
cheat: Malicious .desktop files in /etc/xdg/autostart or ~/.config/autostart with Exec directive pointing to binary | Distinct from cron/systemd: triggers on desktop environment load, not system boot or scheduled time

name: Active Setup
cheat: Registry key HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Active Setup\Installed Components\{GUID}\StubPath containing command | Distinct from Run keys: executes per-user at logon via Internet Explorer setup mechanism, often hidden from standard startup tools

name: Login Items
cheat: Entries in ~/Library/Application Support/com.apple.backgroundtaskmanagementagent/backgrounditems.btm or launchd plists via SMLoginItemSetEnabled | Distinct from LaunchAgents: SMF items are invisible in System Preferences and managed by launchd, while shared list items use LaunchServices

name: Abuse Elevation Control Mechanism
cheat: Abuse of UAC, sudo, or setuid binaries to bypass authorization controls for higher privileges | Distinct from specific exploits: focuses on circumventing OS-native elevation prompts or permission checks rather than kernel vulnerabilities

name: Setuid and Setgid
cheat: Look for binaries with setuid/setgid bits (ls -l shows 's' in exec position) or find commands like 'find / -perm +4000' to locate vulnerable targets. | Distinguish from Sudo (T1548.003): Setuid is a file permission bit on the binary itself, not a command-line privilege delegation tool.

name: Bypass User Account Control
cheat: Monitor for auto-elevating binaries (eventvwr.exe, rundll32.exe) spawning child processes with High Integrity without UAC prompts, or COM object abuse. | Distinguish from standard UAC: This bypasses the user prompt entirely using trusted system binaries or COM interfaces.

name: Sudo and Sudo Caching
cheat: Check /etc/sudoers for 'NOPASSWD' entries or 'Defaults !tty_tickets' modifications, and monitor /var/db/sudo timestamps for cached credential abuse. | Distinguish from Setuid (T1548.001): Sudo relies on configuration files and cached credentials, not file permission bits on binaries.

name: Elevated Execution with Prompt
cheat: Identify calls to the deprecated AuthorizationExecuteWithPrivileges API, often triggered by masquerading installers or modified legitimate apps requesting root credentials. | Distinguish from UAC Bypass (T1548.002): This is macOS-specific and relies on user credential entry via a specific API, not Windows integrity level manipulation.

name: Temporary Elevated Cloud Access
cheat: Review cloud audit logs for Just-In-Time (JIT) access requests, service account impersonation (iam.serviceAccountTokenCreator), or PassRole permissions granting temporary elevated roles. | Distinguish from Additional Cloud Roles (T1098.003): This abuses existing temporary access mechanisms (JIT/Impersonation) rather than permanently assigning new IAM roles.

name: TCC Manipulation
cheat: Check /Library/Application Support/com.apple.TCC/TCC.db for unauthorized entries or SIP disabled state | Look for malicious binaries executed via Finder or AppleScript inheriting Full Disk Access

name: Use Alternate Authentication Material
cheat: Identify authentication events using hashes, Kerberos tickets, or API tokens instead of plaintext passwords | Monitor for lateral movement bypassing MFA via cached credentials in memory or disk

name: Application Access Token
cheat: Detect API calls using OAuth or cloud access tokens (e.g., AWS STS, GCP) without corresponding interactive logins | Look for token usage in SaaS/cloud environments that bypasses password changes or MFA

name: Pass the Hash

name: Pass the Ticket
cheat: Detect Kerberos ticket usage (TGT or service tickets) for lateral movement without password authentication | Look for Golden/Silver Ticket generation or 'Overpass the Hash' creating tickets from NTLM hashes

name: Web Session Cookie
cheat: Look for browser profiles or tools (e.g., Burp, custom scripts) importing valid session cookies (JSESSIONID, AWS cookies) to bypass MFA | Distinct from credential theft: no password used, only the authenticated session token is replayed

name: Unsecured Credentials
cheat: Generic search for plaintext creds in files, registry, or app configs across OSes | Umbrella technique; specific sub-techniques define the exact storage location (files, registry, history)

name: Credentials In Files
cheat: Scan for plaintext passwords in config files, .env, source code, or cloud credential files (e.g., ~/.aws/credentials, /var/run/secrets) | Includes GPP XML files on DCs and container logs with deployment params

name: Credentials in Registry
cheat: Query Windows Registry for 'password' or 'username' strings in HKLM/HKCU (e.g., reg query HKLM /f password /t REG_SZ /s) | Focuses on stored auto-logon or service credentials in registry hives

name: Shell History
cheat: Read ~/.bash_history, ~/.zsh_history, or PowerShell ConsoleHost_history.txt for typed credentials | Distinct from registry: targets command-line history files where users paste passwords as arguments

name: Private Keys
cheat: Search for .key, .pem, .p12, .pfx, .cer, .asc files in ~/.ssh, C:\Users\<user>\.ssh, or device crypto stores | Distinguish from T1552.001 by targeting cryptographic key material rather than generic config files or browser caches

name: Cloud Instance Metadata API
cheat: HTTP requests to 169.254.169.254 from within cloud instances or via SSRF vectors | Distinguish from T1552.001 by targeting live metadata endpoints rather than static files on disk

name: Group Policy Preferences
cheat: Access to SYSVOL share and decryption of GPP XML files using the public AES key | Distinguish from T1552.001 by targeting specific Group Policy Preferences in SYSVOL rather than local user profiles

name: Container API
cheat: Queries to Docker API (2375/2376) or Kubernetes API server for secrets, service accounts, or logs | Distinguish from T1552.001 by interacting with container orchestration APIs rather than filesystem artifacts

name: Chat Messages
cheat: Extraction of credentials from Slack, Teams, Email, or Jira via API, admin portals, or compromised integrations | Distinguish from T1552.001 by targeting live SaaS communication platforms rather than local cached files

name: Subvert Trust Controls
cheat: Look for modifications to file permissions, registry keys, or code-signing certificates that disable trust warnings or allow untrusted execution. | Distinguishes from T1553.002 by focusing on the act of undermining the control mechanism rather than just possessing a valid cert.

name: Gatekeeper Bypass
cheat: Check for removal of com.apple.quarantine xattr, modification of Gatekeeper policy, or execution of apps from USB/curl without quarantine flags. | Key indicator is bypassing the first-run prompt via logic errors or missing quarantine attributes on macOS.

name: Code Signing
cheat: Identify malware or tools signed with valid, non-revoked code signing certificates (often stolen or acquired). | Distinct from T1036.001 (Invalid Code Signature) because the signature is cryptographically valid and trusted by the OS.

name: SIP and Trust Provider Hijacking

name: Install Root Certificate

name: Mark-of-the-Web Bypass

name: Code Signing Policy Modification

name: Compromise Host Software Binary
cheat: Compare hashes of common binaries (SSH, browsers) against known-good baselines to detect IAT hooking or entry-point patching. | Check for package manager version locks (e.g., yum-versionlock) preventing updates of modified binaries.

name: Credentials from Password Stores
cheat: Monitor access to credential stores including browser password databases, password manager vaults, and cloud secrets. | Distinguish from T1555.001: this covers generic stores, while .001 is specific to macOS Keychain.

name: Keychain
cheat: Look for 'security dump-keychain -d' execution or direct reads of ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db. | Requires the user's login password to decrypt; check for Keychain Access app usage or CLI security commands.

name: Securityd Memory

name: Credentials from Web Browsers
cheat: Reading browser DBs (e.g., Chrome `Login Data`) and calling `CryptUnprotectData` or scanning browser process memory | Distinct from T1555.004; targets browser-specific stores rather than OS-wide Credential Manager lockers

name: Windows Credential Manager
cheat: Enumerating `.vcrd` files in `%AppData%\Local\Microsoft\Credentials` or using `vaultcmd.exe`/`CredEnumerateA` | Distinct from T1555.003; focuses on OS-managed lockers for apps/networks, not just browser profiles

name: Password Managers
cheat: Extracting plaintext credentials or master passwords from password manager process memory (e.g., KeePass, 1Password) | Distinct from OS stores; targets third-party encrypted databases unlocked in RAM

name: Cloud Secrets Management Stores
cheat: Executing cloud CLI commands like `aws secretsmanager get-secret-value` or `az key vault secret show` | Distinct from T1552.005; direct API calls to secrets managers, not instance metadata endpoints

name: Modify Authentication Process
cheat: LSASS/SAM/PAM process integrity checks fail or show unexpected code injection | Distinction: Parent technique covering all auth process tampering, not specific to DCs, DLLs, or PAM

name: Domain Controller Authentication
cheat: LSASS on Domain Controller patched to accept a specific backdoor password for any account (Skeleton Key) | Distinction: Targets DC LSASS specifically, persists until reboot, allows auth as any user

name: Password Filter DLL
cheat: Registry key HKLM\System\CurrentControlSet\Control\Lsa\Notification Packages contains unknown DLLs | Distinction: Harvests plaintext passwords via malicious DLLs registered with LSA, distinct from LSASS patching

name: Pluggable Authentication Modules
cheat: Modified /etc/pam.d/* configs or patched pam_unix.so accepting hardcoded credentials | Distinction: Linux/macOS specific, targets PAM stack files/libraries rather than Windows LSASS or registry

name: Network Device Authentication
cheat: Network device OS image patched to check for a hardcoded password before standard auth | Distinction: Targets network device firmware/OS images, bypasses native auth via implanted code check

name: Reversible Encryption
cheat: Check AD userParameters for G$RADIUSCHAP and G$RADIUSCHAPKEY values; verify AllowReversiblePasswordEncryption is disabled via GPO or Set-ADUser. Distinguish from standard hash dumping by the presence of reversible encryption flags and RADIUS-specific keys.

name: Multi-Factor Authentication
cheat: Look for MFA exclusions in Azure AD Conditional Access, new vulnerable MFA registrations, or hosts file edits redirecting MFA endpoints to localhost. Distinguish from T1556.009 by focusing on the MFA mechanism itself rather than broader access policy conditions.

name: Hybrid Identity
cheat: Inspect PTA agent processes (AzureADConnectAuthenticationAgentService) for injected DLLs or AD FS Servicehost configs loading malicious libraries. Distinguish from T1556.006 by targeting the hybrid identity sync/authentication bridge (PTA/ADFS) rather than direct MFA toggles.

name: Network Provider DLL
cheat: Monitor registry keys for new Network Provider DLLs and mpnotify.exe RPC traffic; look for NPLogonNotify() calls capturing cleartext credentials. Distinguish from T1556.005 by the use of the Windows Network Provider API for credential interception rather than AD reversible encryption.

name: Conditional Access Policies
cheat: Audit IAM and IdP policies for added trusted IP ranges, removed MFA requirements, or relaxed device compliance rules in Entra ID, Okta, or AWS/GCP. Distinguish from T1556.006 by modifying the broader conditional access logic (IP, device, risk) rather than just the MFA factor.

name: Adversary-in-the-Middle
cheat: Look for protocol downgrade alerts (SSL/TLS), DNS/ARP/LLMNR redirection, or traffic flowing through unexpected intermediate IPs. | Distinguishes from pure sniffing by the active manipulation of routing or name resolution to force traffic through an attacker node.

name: Name Resolution Poisoning and SMB Relay
cheat: Monitor UDP 5355 (LLMNR), 137 (NBT-NS), and 5353 (mDNS) for unsolicited responses or high-volume queries; check for NTLM relay attempts to LDAP/MSSQL. | Distinct from DNS poisoning as it targets local link-layer name resolution services rather than authoritative DNS zones.

name: ARP Cache Poisoning
cheat: Inspect ARP tables for duplicate MAC addresses mapped to different IPs or unexpected MACs for gateway IPs; look for gratuitous ARP packets. | Differs from DHCP spoofing by targeting Layer 2 address resolution rather than IP address allocation.

name: DHCP Spoofing
cheat: Identify rogue DHCP OFFER/ACK packets from unauthorized MACs or conflicting IP/DNS assignments; watch for DHCP exhaustion via mass DISCOVER floods. | Distinct from ARP poisoning as it manipulates IP configuration and DNS settings rather than direct MAC-to-IP mapping.

name: Evil Twin
cheat: Detect Wi-Fi probe requests for known SSIDs followed by connections to rogue APs with identical SSIDs; look for captive portal redirects or certificate mismatches. | Unique to wireless environments, relying on SSID spoofing and signal strength manipulation rather than wired protocol abuse.

name: Steal or Forge Kerberos Tickets
cheat: klist.exe output showing anomalous ticket types or forged TGTs | Distinction: Parent technique covering ticket theft/forgery; specific sub-techniques (Golden/Silver/Kerberoast/AS-REP) define the exact ticket type and hash source.

name: Golden Ticket
cheat: Forged TGTs with future start times or mismatched encryption types in klist | Distinction: Requires KRBTGT hash; grants domain-wide access; requires KDC interaction for TGS.

name: Silver Ticket
cheat: Forged TGS-REP tickets for specific SPNs without corresponding KDC logs | Distinction: Requires service account hash; limited to specific resource; no KDC interaction needed for ticket creation.

name: Kerberoasting
cheat: High volume of TGS-REQ requests for SPNs with RC4 encryption (etype 23) from single host | Distinction: Targets service accounts with SPNs; uses valid user TGT to request service tickets for offline cracking.

name: AS-REP Roasting

name: Ccache Files
cheat: Look for files named krb5cc_<UID> or krb5.ccache in /tmp or paths defined by KRB5CCNAME; check /etc/krb5.conf for custom locations. name: Inter-Process Communication
cheat: Generic parent technique for IPC abuse; look for unusual parent-child process relationships or data exchange between unrelated processes. name: Component Object Model
cheat: Monitor for COM object instantiation (e.g., via PowerShell New-Object or C++ CoCreateInstance) leading to unexpected process creation or file writes. name: Dynamic Data Exchange
cheat: Inspect Office documents (docx/xlsx) and CSV files for DDE formulas (e.g., =DDEAUTO or =DDEEXEC) or embedded objects triggering command execution. name: XPC Services

name: Archive Collected Data
cheat: Look for compression/encryption processes (zip, tar, 7z, openssl) running on collected data files shortly before network egress. Distinguish from exfil by the local file transformation step rather than the transfer itself.

name: Archive via Utility
cheat: Detect execution of standard utilities like tar, zip, diantz, makecab, or 7-Zip creating .zip/.cab/.rar files. Key indicator is the presence of these specific binary names in process logs rather than library calls.

name: Archive via Library
cheat: Identify in-process compression via libraries like zlib, libzip, or Python rarfile without spawning external archive executables. Distinguish from utility-based archiving by the absence of child processes for compression.

name: Archive via Custom Method
cheat: Observe custom encryption/compression logic (e.g., XOR, stream ciphers) implemented directly in malware code without external tool dependencies. Look for high-entropy file outputs lacking standard archive headers.

name: Disk Wipe
cheat: Monitor for raw disk writes, MBR overwrites, or 'erase' commands on network devices. Distinguish from data destruction by the targeting of boot sectors or full sector wipes rather than specific file deletion.

name: Disk Content Wipe
cheat: Direct disk I/O overwriting arbitrary sectors with random data, often via third-party drivers like RawDisk or direct device access. | Distinguishes from Data Destruction by erasing raw disk sectors rather than individual files.

name: Disk Structure Wipe
cheat: Overwriting Master Boot Record (MBR) or partition tables to prevent OS boot; on network devices, use of CLI 'format' commands. | Distinguishes from Disk Content Wipe by targeting specific boot structures rather than arbitrary data sectors.

name: Remote Service Session Hijacking
cheat: Taking control of an already-established remote session (SSH, RDP, Telnet) instead of initiating a new login. | Distinguishes from Remote Services by hijacking existing connections rather than creating new ones with valid credentials.

name: SSH Hijacking
cheat: Accessing the SSH agent socket or compromising the agent process to reuse active public key authentication sessions. | Distinguishes from standard SSH lateral movement by hijacking existing authenticated sessions rather than logging in anew.

name: RDP Hijacking
cheat: Executing 'c:\windows\system32\tscon.exe [session_id]' with SYSTEM privileges to steal active or disconnected RDP sessions. | Distinguishes from standard RDP login by hijacking existing sessions without requiring user credentials or prompts.

name: Hide Artifacts
cheat: Parent technique for evading detection by hiding files, users, or windows using OS features. | Look for artifacts isolated from standard security instrumentation or hidden via native OS mechanisms.

name: Hidden Files and Directories
cheat: Files/dirs hidden via dot-prefix (Linux/macOS), attrib.exe (Windows), or space-only names. | macOS UF_HIDDEN flag hides from Finder but not Terminal; verify with ls -a or dir /a.

name: Hidden Users
cheat: Windows: HKLM\...\SpecialAccounts\UserList value 0 hides user from logon screen. | macOS: Hide500Users TRUE in loginwindow plist or dscl IsHidden 1; Linux: gsettings disable-user-list true.

name: Hidden Window
cheat: Windows: powershell -WindowStyle Hidden, off-screen WindowPosition registry, or CreateDesktop API for hidden desktops. | macOS: apple.awt.UIElement plist tag hides Dock icon; check for invisible GUI processes.

name: NTFS File Attributes
cheat: Malicious data stored in NTFS Alternate Data Streams (ADS) or Extended Attributes (EA) within MFT. | Use Get-Item -Stream * or stream tools to reveal hidden payloads invisible to standard file scanners.

name: Hidden File System
cheat: Look for files stored in reserved disk space, portable partition images dropped as regular files, or fragmented file structures bypassing standard FS metadata. | Distinguish from standard hidden files by checking for non-standard partition layouts or data hidden in VBR/MFT structures.

name: Run Virtual Instance
cheat: Detect rogue VMs via /bin/vmx execution on ESXi, .wsb config files on Windows, or QEMU/VirtualBox processes; check for shared folders bridging guest/host. | Distinguish from legitimate virtualization by identifying VMs absent from vCenter console or created via direct ESXi file manipulation.

name: VBA Stomping
cheat: Inspect Office docs for zeroed/benign VBA source code while compiled p-code remains active in module streams. | Distinguish from standard macro malware by verifying if source code matches executed p-code or if source is intentionally obfuscated to bypass static scans.

name: Email Hiding Rules
cheat: Audit mailbox rules for keywords like 'malware' or 'phish' that auto-delete/move emails; check New-InboxRule/Set-InboxRule PowerShell logs and Exchange transport rules. | Distinguish from user-created rules by identifying rules targeting security alert content or C2 communication patterns.

name: Resource Forking
cheat: Use ls -l@ or xattr -l to reveal resource forks containing hidden executables or data on macOS files. | Distinguish from standard extended attributes by identifying executable payloads or obfuscated code stored in the resource fork rather than the data fork.

name: Process Argument Spoofing
cheat: Process PEB command-line arguments differ from initial creation logs or are overwritten via WriteProcessMemory | Distinguish from Process Hollowing by checking if args change after process resume or if PEB is patched post-execution

name: Ignore Process Interrupts
cheat: Processes launched with nohup, disown, or PowerShell -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue to ignore SIGHUP/interrupts | Unlike Trap, this does not create persistence but prevents termination on session logout or C2 drop

name: File/Path Exclusions
cheat: Malicious files dropped in default AV exclusion paths (e.g., C:\Windows\Temp, %APPDATA%) without modifying AV config | Distinct from Disable or Modify Tools as it leverages pre-existing hardcoded scanner exclusions

name: Bind Mounts
cheat: Linux bind mounts overlaying benign /proc/[pid] onto malicious /proc/[pid] to hide process metadata from ps/top | Look for mount -o bind commands targeting /proc directories to mask executable paths and arguments

name: Extended Attributes
cheat: Payloads embedded in file extended attributes (xattrs) using xattr/setfattr, invisible to standard ls/cat/hash checks | Inspect with xattr -p or getfattr --only-values to find hidden second-stage loaders in user. or com.apple. namespaces

name: Data Manipulation
cheat: Integrity threat via insertion, deletion, or modification of data to influence outcomes or hide activity. | Requires specialized expertise and access to target-specific software for complex systems.

name: Stored Data Manipulation
cheat: Manipulation of data at rest including Office files, databases, and stored emails. | Distinguished from transmitted data by targeting files on disk rather than network packets.

name: Transmitted Data Manipulation
cheat: Alteration of data en route to storage or other systems via network interception or process-to-process tools. | Distinguished from stored data by targeting the transmission mechanism rather than the final file state.

name: Runtime Data Manipulation
cheat: Modification of application binaries or file associations to alter data as accessed and displayed to the user. | Distinguished from stored data by manipulating the runtime display layer rather than the underlying file content.

name: Phishing
cheat: Email headers show spoofed sender, missing DKIM/SPF, or thread-hijack patterns; attachments contain macros, embedded objects, or links to malicious URLs | Distinguish from T1566.002 (Spearphishing Link) by presence of executable payload vs. URL redirect, and from T1566.001 (Spearphishing Attachment) by file-based delivery

name: Spearphishing Attachment
